title: What is the difference between persist() and merge() in JPA, and how does Spring Data's save() relate to merge()?

s1_definition.profdef: `persist()` makes a NEW transient entity managed and schedules an INSERT; it returns void and throws if the entity already exists in the persistence context with the same id. `merge()` copies the state of a detached (or new) entity into a managed instance and returns that managed copy; the argument you pass in is NOT managed afterwards. Spring Data's `save()` delegates to `persist()` for new entities and `merge()` for existing ones based on whether the id is null or the @Version is unset.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Rajesh walking into National Bank of India with a brand new account-opening form. `persist()` is the clerk stamping that exact form and filing it — the form Rajesh holds becomes the official record. `merge()` is different: Rajesh brings a photocopy of an old form with edits scribbled on it; the clerk does NOT file the photocopy, instead the clerk pulls the official file, copies Rajesh's edits onto it, and files that. Rajesh's photocopy stays unofficial. Spring Data's `save()` is the smart front-desk person who looks at whether you already have an account number, then decides to either file a new form or copy edits onto the existing file.
s1_definition.oneliner: persist attaches the SAME object; merge copies state into a DIFFERENT managed object and returns it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `persist()` makes a NEW transient entity managed and schedules an INSERT; it returns void and throws if the entity already exists in the persistence context with the same id. `merge()` copies the state of a detached (or new) entity into a managed instance and returns that managed copy; the argument you pass in is NOT managed afterwards. Spring Data's `save()` delegates to `persist()` for new entities and `merge()` for existing ones based on whether the id is null or the @Version is unset.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Rajesh walking into National Bank of India with a brand new account-opening form. `persist()` is the clerk stamping that exact form and filing it — the form Rajesh holds becomes the official record. `merge()` is different: Rajesh brings a photocopy of an old form with edits scribbled on it; the clerk does NOT file the photocopy, instead the clerk pulls the official file, copies Rajesh's edits onto it, and files that. Rajesh's photocopy stays unofficial. Spring Data's `save()` is the smart front-desk person who looks at whether you already have an account number, then decides to either file a new form or copy edits onto the existing file.

**One line to remember:** persist attaches the SAME object; merge copies state into a DIFFERENT managed object and returns it.

sections.s2_technical:
`persist(entity)` takes a transient entity and makes it managed. For example, when Rajesh opens a new account: `entityManager.persist(rajeshAccount)` schedules an INSERT and the passed object `rajeshAccount` itself becomes managed, so later changes to it are tracked by dirty checking. It returns void. If you call persist on a detached entity (one that has an id but is no longer managed), Hibernate throws `PersistenceException`.

`merge(entity)` is for detached entities. Suppose an account object was loaded in a previous transaction, serialized to a web layer, edited, and sent back. That object is now detached. Calling `Account managed = entityManager.merge(detachedAccount)` loads (or finds in context) the current managed instance, copies the detached state onto it, and returns the managed instance. The key trap: `detachedAccount` stays detached — you must use the RETURNED object: `managed.setBalance(...)`.

`save()` in Spring Data JPA (`SimpleJpaRepository.save`) checks `isNew(entity)`. For example, if the id is null or the @Version field is null, it calls `em.persist(entity)` and returns the same instance; otherwise it calls `em.merge(entity)` and returns the merged managed instance. A senior-level nuance: because save() may return a DIFFERENT object via merge, always reassign: `account = repo.save(account)`.

Another nuance: `persist` participates in transactional write-behind — the INSERT may not hit the database until flush. `merge` may trigger a SELECT first (to load the managed state) unless the entity is already in the context, which is why bulk updates via merge can be slower than a direct JPQL UPDATE.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India opens a brand new savings account for Rajesh. There is no record yet; we must create one. This is exactly how `persist()` works — it takes a fresh object with no database row and inserts it, keeping that same object managed so any further edits in the same transaction are saved automatically.

Problem 2 — Priya's current account details were loaded this morning, sent to the mobile app, and she edited her registered address. The app sends back the whole account object. In our service it arrives DETACHED — Hibernate does not track it. If we just set fields and save, we risk overwriting fields we did not mean to. This is exactly how `merge()` works — it copies the incoming detached state onto the live managed record and returns the managed one.

Problem 3 — The team uses Spring Data `save()` everywhere and someone noticed that after `repo.save(account)` the original variable sometimes does not reflect the generated id. This is because save() used merge() internally and returned a different instance. The fix is to always use the returned value.

We will build an AccountService with `openAccount()` (persist), `updateFromDetached()` (merge), and a demo showing save()'s dual behaviour.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/account-persistence-service-1.0.0.jar

# Open a new account (persist path)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"id":"SAV2001","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1000000}'

# Update detached (merge path)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/CUR3001 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"id":"CUR3001","address":"New Address, Mumbai"}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: open account `SAV2001` for Rajesh with 1,000,000, then merge a detached `CUR3001` with a new address.

Step 1 — `openAccount("SAV2001", ...)` creates a transient Account. At this point it exists only in Java memory; no database row.

Step 2 — `em.persist(acc)` makes `acc` managed and schedules an INSERT in the persistence context (not yet flushed). The same `acc` object is now tracked.

Step 3 — `acc.setAddress("Branch default")` changes a field on the managed object. Dirty checking notes the change.

Step 4 — On transaction commit, Hibernate flushes: one INSERT (with the address already set, so no separate UPDATE in this case because the change happened before flush).

Step 5 — For the merge path, the detached `CUR3001` arrives. `em.merge(detached)` issues a SELECT (CUR3001 not in context), builds a managed copy, copies the new address onto it, and returns the managed instance. The original `detached` object stays detached.

Step 6 — On commit, Hibernate flushes a single UPDATE changing the address from "Old Address, Pune" to "New Address, Mumbai".

```
INFO  Opened account SAV2001 via persist()
Hibernate: insert into accounts (holder_name,balance,address,status,id) values (?,?,?,?,?)
INFO  Merged account CUR3001; detached==managed? false
Hibernate: select ... from accounts where id=?
Hibernate: update accounts set address=? where id=?
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core difference is identity. `persist()` takes a brand new transient entity, schedules an INSERT, and the exact object you passed in becomes managed, so later field changes are tracked by dirty checking. It returns nothing and will fail if you hand it a detached entity. `merge()` is built for detached entities: it loads or finds the live managed instance, copies your detached object's state onto it, and returns that managed instance. The object you passed to merge stays detached, which is the single biggest gotcha — you must always work with the returned value.

Spring Data JPA's `save()` sits on top of both. Internally it checks whether the entity is new, typically by looking at a null id or a null @Version field. If it is new, save delegates to persist and returns the same instance. If it is not new, save delegates to merge and returns a possibly different managed instance. Because of this I always write `account = repository.save(account)` so I never lose the generated id or managed state.

In our National Bank of India system, when Rajesh opens a fresh savings account I use persist because there is no existing row and I want the same object to stay managed through the transaction. When Priya edits her address in the mobile app and sends the whole account object back, it arrives detached, so I use merge, and I carefully use the returned managed object. The performance nuance I mention in interviews is that merge can trigger an extra SELECT to load the managed state, so for large bulk updates I prefer a direct JPQL UPDATE instead of loading and merging thousands of detached objects.

This understanding matters in banking because overwriting fields you did not intend to change can corrupt financial records. Merge copies the entire state of the detached object, so if the mobile app sent a stale balance along with the new address, merge would happily overwrite the balance too. That is why in production I map only the fields I intend to change rather than blindly merging whole entities from the client.

---

keyPoints: persist(): attach NEW entity to context — INSERT on flush
merge(): copy detached entity state into managed copy — UPDATE on flush
persist() fails on detached entity, merge() handles both new and detached
save() in Spring Data: delegates to persist (new) or merge (existing)
